case_name: Woolworth Canada Inc. v. Human Rights Commission (Nfld.) and White
text:
Woolworth Canada Inc. v. Newfoundland (Human Rights Comm.)

1993-12-02

Newfoundland and Labrador Supreme Court

Woolworth Canada Inc.

Plaintiff

v.

Newfoundland Human Rights Commission and Thomas White

Defendants

Date of Decision:

December 2, 1993

Before:

Newfoundland Supreme Court Trial Division, Orsborn J.

Court File No.:

1993 St.J. No. 3651

Appealed by:

(1995), 25 C.H.R.R. D227 (Nfld. C.A.)

Appearances by:

Ian F. Kelly, Counsel for the Plaintiff

B. Gale Welsh, Counsel for the Commission

Michael J. Crosbie, Counsel for the Defendant Thomas White

APPEALS AND JUDICIAL REVIEW — human rights commission's decision to appoint a board of inquiry — HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSIONS — appointment process — PROCEDURE — procedural fairness — PRODUCTION OF DOCUMENTS — investigation report

SETTLEMENT — responsibility of human rights commission for failure to reach a settlement — JURISDICTION — adequate effort to effect a settlement — reasonable apprehension of bias — COSTS — costs arising from human rights commission acting irresponsibly in pursuing complaint — INTERPRETATION OF STATUTES — definition of "because of" and "shall"

DISABILITY — employment terminated on the basis of back condition — disabled employee's ability to return to work — DISCRIMINATION — adverse effect discrimination — direct discrimination — ability to work — definition of discrimination — REASONABLE ACCOMMODATION — duty to accommodate short of undue hardship — statutory duty to accommodate — BONA FIDE OCCUPATIONAL QUALIFICATION —
bona fide
occupational qualification

Summary:
This is an application for an order quashing the decision of the Newfoundland Human Rights Commission to appoint a Board of Inquiry to hear and decide the complaint of Thomas White that he was discriminated against because of a disability.

Mr. White worked for Woolworth Canada Inc. (Woolco) for twenty-four years. In April 1990 he injured his back at work and could not perform his job. He had surgery several times, and was unable to work until July 1993. However, Woolco terminated Mr. White's employment in February 1991.

Mr. White filed a complaint alleging that he was discriminated against because of a disability by being dismissed from his employment.

The issues in this proceeding are: 1) is an examination of the circumstances surrounding Mr. White's termination within the jurisdiction of a Board of Inquiry under the Code; 2) is the Commission required to attempt to settle a complaint as a precondition to appointing a Board of Inquiry, and was such an attempt made; and 3) did the Commission act fairly and without creating a reasonable apprehension of bias in its dealings with White and Woolco prior to appointing a Board of Inquiry?

The Supreme Court of Newfoundland, Trial Division, finds that the complaint was not within the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry. White was terminated because he was incapable of doing his job, and of doing any work at the time. Termination because of inability to do the job cannot be considered discrimination on the basis of disability. The Court repudiates the Commission's argument that the question of whether White's termination was discriminatory is a question that falls squarely within the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry and should not be decided by the Court. It finds that it is undisputed that White was terminated because he was incapable of doing his job, and this fact takes his complaint outside the ambit of s. 9 of the Code. White was not terminated "because of" disability, and the employer's action was not based on a prohibited ground.

The Court finds that there is no direct discrimination because of disability, and there is no adverse effect discrimination either. The rule that affected White is the inferred rule that Woolco employees must be capable of coming to work and doing the job for which they were hired. Any such rule is aimed at ability to do the job, and it does not adversely affect any individual because of a prohibited ground of discrimination.

The Court concludes that White was not terminated because of a prohibited ground and a Board of Inquiry has no jurisdiction to adjudicate his complaint.

The Court also finds that the Commission is required to make attempts to settle a complaint before appointing a Board of Inquiry, and it did not make such attempts adequately in this case. Commission representatives met with Thomas White and his counsel, but were unable to obtain his agreement to settlement terms which they proposed. Since Mr. White's agreement could not be obtained, the Commission did not make settlement attempts with Woolco. The Court finds that presenting a suggestion to one party and then giving up when that party rejects the suggestion does not satisfy the obligation imposed by the Code. Therefore, the statutory obligation to try to bring about a settlement was not satisfied in this case.

Finally, the Court finds that the Commission gave Thomas White and his counsel opportunities to see an investigator's report and a solicitor's memorandum, and invited them to make a written submission to the Commission, while the same opportunities were not afforded to the respondent Woolco. These actions breached the requirements of procedural fairness and raised a reasonable apprehension of bias in the decision to appoint a Board of Inquiry.

The Court quashes the decision of the Commission to appoint a Board of Inquiry, and prohibits it from proceeding further with the complaint. It also orders the Commission to pay the costs of both the complainant and the respondent.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]    Thomas White was employed by Woolworth Canada ("Woolco") at its Village Mall store in St. John's. He was injured at work in April 1990 and could not perform his job. He received Workers' Compensation benefits on the basis of total disability. On February 22, 1991, Woolco terminated White's employment. He continued to receive Workers' Compensation benefits and has continued to do so until the hearing of this application.

[
2
]    White filed a complaint with the Human Rights Commission (the "Commission") on August 19, 1991, alleging discrimination on the basis of physical disability, and therefore a contravention of para. 9(1)(a) of the
Human Rights Code,
R.S.N. 1990, c. H-14 (the "
Code
"). He also commenced an action for wrongful dismissal. Judgment awarding Mr. White twelve months' notice was filed on May 12, 1993.

[
3
]    On March 25, 1993, following an investigation, the Commission
referred
White
's complaint to a board of inquiry. Woolco has applied for an order quashing the Commission's decision to refer the complaint to a board of inquiry, and prohibiting the Commission from proceeding further with the complaint.

ISSUES

4 1.    Is an examination of the circumstances of White's termination within the jurisdiction of a board of inquiry constituted under the
Code?

2.    Is the Commission required by the
Code
to attempt to effect a settlement of the complaint as a precondition to appointing a board of inquiry; if so, was such an attempt made in this case?

3.    Did the Commission act fairly and without creating a reasonable apprehension of bias in its dealings with the complainant White prior to constituting a board of inquiry?

I will deal with each issue separately.

Issue No. 1

5    Is an examination of the circumstances of White's termination within the jurisdiction of a board of inquiry constituted under the
Code?

Positions of the Parties

[6]    Woolco
stated that
White
was terminated because he was incapable of doing his job. He was not only incapable of doing his particular job at Woolco, but of doing any work. At the time of his termination, there was no indication from White of when, if ever, he would be capable of doing his job. Woolco argued that termination because of a complete inability to do the job cannot be considered discrimination on account of physical disability. Because the facts are uncontradicted, there are no facts which could amount to discrimination, and hence no possible breach of the
Code.
Accordingly, there is no jurisdiction in the Commission to constitute a board of inquiry.

[7]    The Commission, supported by
White
, argued
that the determination of whether or not there was discrimination lies at the hearing of the Board's jurisdiction. An order of prohibition would stop the Board from fulfilling the very essence of its mandate — the question of whether or not circumstances which are the subject of a complaint are discriminatory and thereby contravene the
Code.

Facts

[8]    On April 7, 1990, White injured his back at work. He had been employed with Woolco for about twenty-four years. White received, and has continued to receive, Workers' Compensation benefits on the basis of total disability. He has received the maximum permissible compensation under workers' compensation legislation.

[9]    From April 17, 1990, until February 22, 1991, Woolco "topped up" White's Workers' Compensation benefits to his full salary.

[10]    On February 4, 1991, Woolco wrote to White:

February 4, 1991
Mr. Thomas White
35 O'Flaherty Cr.
Mount Pearl, Newfoundland
A1N 4M4

Dear Thomas

Our records indicate you have been receiving Workman's Compensation benefits since April 9, 1990.

It was our intention that you would assume the responsibility of Section Manager when you were appointed to the position on May 1, 1989, but the recurring back injury seems to suggest that you will be unable to assume that role.

As you are aware we must continue to operate our business and protect our market share. It is by way of this letter that we are serving notice.

We expect that Thomas White will assume his duties of Section Manager in #6399 on or before February 22, 1991. Failure to assume that position on or before February 22, 1991 will be taken as your resignation.

We sincerely hope that you will assume your role in #6399 and regret being forced to take this action, but are forced to protect our business in St. John's.

Yours truly

(Sgd.) J.R. Thompson

J.R. THOMPSON
MANAGER OF MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT

cc. P. RATZLAFF
T. MAKING
J. GUERTIN

[11]    On March 15, 1991, White's solicitors wrote to Woolco. The letter read in part:

We can now advise that we understand from Mr. White that his doctor has recommended that surgery be performed concerning a pinched nerve in his back; however, before this surgery can be performed, Mr. White has to lose some weight and undergo a program of physiotherapy and exercise. Only once the surgery is performed will the doctors be able to decide whether, when and to what extent Mr. White can return to work ...

In addition, we can confirm that Mr. White has not and does not intend to resign from his position as Section Manager. In fact, it is Mr. White's intention to recommence his duties as Section Manager as soon as he can.

[12]    On August 19, 1991, White filed his complaint with the Commission, alleging discrimination because of physical disability. His complaint read in part:

I am still waiting to go in for surgery. The Health Science Hospital told me they will call [
sic
] when to go in.

Some of the Miller Centre recommendations are:

1.    To lose weight

2.    Increase general activity e.g. swimming, walking etc.

I am unable to go back to work until this happens and more therapy after surgery.

[13]    White's solicitors again wrote to Woolco on August 23, 1991:

Both in February, 1991 and today Mr. White wishes to return to work, but his doctors will not allow him to do so until he has successfully completed a course of medical treatment. That medical treatment is still ongoing. You should note that no doctor has stated that Mr. White will be unable to return to work due to his injury at Woolworth's. There are no grounds for dismissing Mr. White ...

Clearly, Woolworth's has terminated Mr. White's employment contract because of his physical disability, his bad back. Woolworth's has dismissed Mr. White because he is on Workers' Compensation instead of being at work. Clearly Woolworth's is treating Mr. White differently from other employees who can only be dismissed for just cause whereas Mr. White has been dismissed because of his bad back and because of the fact that he is on Workers' Compensation.

[14]    On November 13, 1991, White's solicitors forwarded to the Commission a medical report by Dr. F. Maroun:

This patient was seen by me initially in 1988 at the request of Dr. Neil Turner, for investigation of back and leg pain. He was admitted under my service in 1988:01:13.

His initial injury had occurred in 1987, around May, when he was lifting some carpet, and immediately after he felt pain in the back and at that time in both legs. He was treated conservatively, but he did not improve and subsequently in 1988:01:14, he was operated upon when a disc was removed from the level of L4-L5 on the left side.

He did well and then in April, after going back to work he sustained another injury while lifting. His pain was in the back and leg. He was admitted to the General Hospital on July 8, 1990 ... We did not feel that surgery was indicated.

We treated him with a special brace ... His pain continued and persisted in the back and the leg and Dr. A.E. Shapter had seen him and we have discussed the problems together regarding the management of this patient, and we both felt that he is disabled and to relieve his pain, we have advised an exploration of the nerve root and fusion. He is presently on the waiting list to be admitted for this.

I do not think that even if the fusion is successful he would be able to go back to his heavy work duty; however, one can't tell until he tries it, if his surgery is successful in alleviating his pain.

[15]
White
provided
the Commission with a statement on February 11, 1992:

I had a spinal fusion of S1, L5, L4 lower back and discs. The surgery was successful. The operation took place on December 9 '91. My progress is unknown at this point. I have to see Dr. Shapter on April 24, 1992. It is hoped that with time my back will be as good as new.

[16]    Commission Executive Director Gladys Vivian noted on February 25, 1992:

I telephoned Mr. White, after reviewing files as I saw no indication as to when he would be able to return to work. Mr. White says he had surgery on December 9/91 and has no indication, at present, as to when he would be available to return to work. [Initialled G.V.]

[17]    Commission Investigator Patricia Corbett noted on June 25, 1992:

Mr. White will accept his job back as part of the settlement. He also wants the benefits, holidays, pensions etc.

Mr. White has not yet been cleared to return to work.

Ms. Corbett's investigator's report of July 2, 1992, included:

Because of the seriousness of the injury, Mr. White had a spinal fusion of S1, L5 & L4 lower back and disc. The surgery was successful and it is hoped that with time and therapy Mr. White "will be as good as new."

[18]    The Commission's notes of a meeting with White in September 1992 include:

4.    Tom has not worked or sought work since his injury. He was unable to do either.

5.    He has [made] no effort to do or find alternate employ[ment] because he was unable to do so because of injury.

And on November 25:

Tom White — spoke to Tom to get an update — Dr. Shapter wants him to continue therapy until March. He will not see Dr. Shapter until then, so I guess it is safe to assume he will not be fit for work until March at least.

[19]    Ms. Corbett forwarded this information to the Commission's solicitor on November 25, 1992. In particular, Ms. Corbett advised:

1.    Mr. White saw Dr. Shapter in November of 1992. He is progressing well but Dr. Shapter feels that Mr. White should have more therapy on his back to make it stronger. He is to continue therapy until he sees Dr. Shapter again in March 1993.

2.    Up to this point in time Mr. White has not had any discussions with his coun[se]llors at Workers' Compensation Commission about retraining. Up to this point it hasn't been an issue as he has been unable to do any kind of work.

3.    Mr. White is still in receipt of workers' compensation.

4.    Tom has not worked or sought other different work since his injury. He was unable to do either.

5.    No effort has been made to find alternate employment because of his injury. Mr. White will take Dr. Shapter's advice about the kind of employment he will be able to do, when he is declared medically fit.

[20]    On March 16, 1993, White's solicitors sent a submission to the Commission. It read, in part:

Imagine yourself in Thomas White's position ...

Through no fault of your own, it takes 9 months for you to be able to obtain access to a hospital bed, an operating room and a surgeon.

Your surgery is successful and after about 13 months of convalescence you are able to go through work hardening at the Miller Centre.

After close to 3 years, you will be able to return to work, but now you have no job and are faced with the very difficult task of finding employment when competing with able bodied workers for scarce jobs in Newfoundland.

What employer is going to hire you when you tell him that you are 44 years of age and have been off work for the last 3 years due to a back injury?

[21]    A Statement of Facts attached to the Solicitor's Submission says:

20.  Through no fault of his own, it was not until December 1991 that the Plaintiff was able to have his surgery on his lumbar spine. In August 1992 Dr. Shapter reported to the Workers' Compensation Commis- sion that Thomas White was doing "very well" and that his fusion was "solid." At that time, Dr. Shapter recommended that a rehabilitation approach should be taken and he stated that the Plaintiff is "a very aggressive and intelligent man and I think that he will do very well with any program which can be offered to him."

21.  As of the beginning of 1993, the Plaintiff has been attending the Miller Centre for reconditioning and work hardening and it is anticipated that he will be able to commence a job search in the near future.

[22]    On March 25, 1993, the Commission
referred
White
's complaint to a board of inquiry.

[23]    Concurrently with his human rights complaint, White pursued his civil action in court. By decision filed on May 12, 1993, Mr. Justice Riche concluded that, in view of the circumstances prevailing when the notice of termination was given, White's employment contract had not been frustrated. At pp. 7–8 of the judgment (1991 St.J. No. 4032 [reported
1993 CanLII 8415 (NL SC)
,
109 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 187
]):

... We know from hindsight that the Plaintiff in this case has been disabled for more than three years, and I do not know with any certainty when and if he will be able to return to his former type of work. To determine whether or not there is frustration, I must apply my mind to the circumstances prevailing at the time the notice was given. That was February of 1990, some ten months after the disability arose. At that time, through communications between the employer and the employee, it was understood that Mr. White was still disabled and would require an operation on his back to remedy that problem. When this surgery was to be performed depended upon physicians and hospital time being available. I suppose it was possible that he could have had his operation within the next month and have recovered and have been ready for employment within a year. We know now, however, through hindsight that it was ten months before and five months has passed since his operation, and he is still not able to return to work. There is no evidence to suggest that the employer knew that White would take so long to recover.

Riche J. concluded that White was entitled to twelve months' notice — because of offsetting benefits the amount due to White was calculated at $730.68. He was not awarded his costs.

[24]    White filed an affidavit in this proceeding:

6.   At the time of the wrongful dismissal trial before Judge [
sic
] Riche in the first week of May 1993, I had had a successful back fusion but was experiencing a complication called tarsal tunnel syndrome wherein there was swelling in my ankle, the remedy for which was some surgery on my ankle, which surgery could have complications but if successful, would involve about three weeks of recovery time and this is why Judge [
sic
] Riche stated in his decision that I was still not able to return to work at my former position as a sales manager, but even then I was quite capable of light employment duties.

7.   I had successful surgery on my ankle in June 1993 and if Woolworth had been cooperative, I could have gone back to my sales manager's position with Woolworth certainly by August 1993.

35.  Since July 1993, I have been fully able to perform the duties outlined in the job description concerning the position which I had with Woolworth when I injured myself in April 1990 ...

The Code

25      9(1) An employer, or a person acting on behalf of an employer, shall not refuse to employ or to continue to employ or otherwise discriminate against a person in regard to employment or a term or condition of employment because of

(a)    that person's race, religion, religious creed, political opinion, colour or ethnic, national or social origin, sex, marital status, physical disability or mental disability; or

(b)    that person's age, if that person has reached the age of 19 years and has not reached the age of 65 years,

but this subsection does not apply to the expression of a limitation, specification or preference based on a good faith occupational qualification.

20(1) A person who had reasonable grounds for believing that a person has contravened this Act may file with the executive director a complaint in a form acceptable to the commission.

Analysis

26    A complaint is predicated on reasonable grounds for believing that the
Code
has been contravened. White alleged a contravention of para. 9(1)(a) — a refusal to continue to employ because of physical disability.

[27]    Woolco argued that White was terminated because he was incapable of doing the job. Termination for this reason does not contravene the
Code.
There is no basis for a complaint and hence no basis for the appointment of a board of inquiry. The Commission took the position that the question for determination is a question of fact that falls squarely within the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry. Whether or not White's termination was discriminatory is a question for the Board and not for this Court on a prohibition proceeding.

[28]    Counsel for Woolco suggested that the situation is similar to that
considered by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Bell
v.
Ontario Human Rights Commission
,

1971 CanLII 195 (SCC)
,
[1971] S.C.R. 756
. The Ontario legislation did not extend to accommodation issues involving other than "self-contained" dwelling units. Faced with a complaint alleging a discriminatory refusal to rent certain living accommodation, the landlord sought prohibition on the grounds that the dwelling unit in question was not a self-contained dwelling unit, and hence not within the ambit of the legislation. By a majority, the Supreme Court of Canada agreed with the landlord and restored the trial judge's order of prohibition.

[29]    In the course of his judgment, Martland J. said at p. 768:

If a complaint of alleged discrimination is made, which relates to a field which is not within the provisions of the Act, has the Supreme Court of Ontario the power, by an order of prohibition, to prevent proceedings for the investigation of the complaint under s. 13 of the Act?

But the Act is specifically limited by its terms to dealing with such discrimination when it occurs in relation to defined fields of operation ...

At p. 769:

The task of a board of inquiry appointed by the Minister is to investigate "the matter," i.e., to determine whether, in a matter within the purview of the Act, there has been discrimination.

In the present case the Commission was of the stated opinion that the complaint was one of discrimination contrary to the Act, and for that reason it recommended the appointment by the Minister of a board of inquiry. The respondent was convinced that the complaint did not relate to a matter within the purview of the Act. Is he precluded from having that vital issue determined in a court of law without waiting until the inquiry is conducted and until the board has determined that issue?

At p. 775:

The powers given to a board of inquiry are to enable it to determine whether or not there has been discrimination in respect of matters within the scope of the Act. It has no power to deal with alleged discrimination in matters not within the purview of the Act or to make recommendations with respect there to.

[Whether the accommodation was covered by the
Code
] raises an issue of law respecting the scope of the operation of the Act, and on the answer to that question depends the authority of the board to inquire into the complaint of discrimination at all. The Act does not purport to place that issue within the exclusive jurisdiction of the board, and a wrong decision on it would not enable the board to proceed further.

[30]    It is evident that
Bell, supra,
was not dealing with the issue of whether or not the denial of housing was on a prohibited ground. Rather, the issue was whether or not the activity or subject matter — the housing — came within the legislation in the first place. By analogy, if one were dealing with this case with a volunteer rather than an employee, the issue may arise whether or not volunteers were subject to the legislation.

[31]    The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal commented on the limited scope of
Bell
in
Re CIP Paper Products Limited and Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission

(1978),
1978 CanLII 1847 (SK CA)
,
87 D.L.R. (3d) 609
at 612
:

Care must be taken not to give to the decision in
Bell
v.
Ontario Human Rights Com'n, supra,
too wide an application. That case simply decided that, where there is a clear point of law not depending upon particular facts upon the determination of which the jurisdiction of the tribunal depends, that determination may be made in an application for prohibition. That judgment did not decide that prohibition lies on the contention that the complaint is one which cannot be sustained within the provisions of the Act in respect to which the complaint is made. The decision as to whether the complaint is one which is contemplated by the pertinent legislation, and, if so, whether discrimination is, or is not, established, are matters for the Human Rights Commission. Such statutory rights and duties of the Commission cannot be usurped by the Court under the guise of prohibition proceedings in which is sought, in effect, a determination of the complaint on its merits.

[32]    A slightly more flexible approach was taken by the New Brunswick Court of Appeal in
Board of Education
v.
Human Rights Board of Inquiry (N.B.)

(1989),
1989 CanLII 208 (NB CA)
,
100 N.B.R. (2d) 181
[10 C.H.R.R. D/6426] (C.A.); leave to appeal refused
104 N.R. 318 (S.C.C.)
. Stratton C.J.N.B. said at p. 193 [D/6429, para. 45399]:

An application for judicial review to prohibit an administrative tribunal from proceeding may be sought as soon as an absence of jurisdiction has either arisen or may clearly be foreseen. The main advantage of such an application is that it may be brought to test the validity of proceedings before they are undertaken with a possible saving of time and expense ... The guiding principle would seem to be that where there is a clear question of law not depending upon particular facts, there is no reason why an applicant should not go directly to the court for a judicial review order prohibiting a tribunal from proceeding rather than waiting to see if the decision goes against him, in which case he would then have to move to quash the decision ...

[33]    After reviewing the
Bell
and
CIP Paper
decisions,
supra,
Chief Justice Stratton said at p. 195 [D/6429, para. 45402]:

It is perhaps trite to note that there are numerous authoritative decisions which have directed courts to exercise restraint and curial deference when dealing with the specialized jurisdiction confided to statutory tribunals. It has been said that a court ought not to preempt a statutory tribunal nor usurp its rights and duties under the guise of prohibition proceedings. Nor should a court be astute to hold that Parliament did not intend the tribunal to have jurisdiction to decide for itself the meaning of ordinary words used in the statute to define the question which it has to decide. On the other hand, it has also been said that it is a jurisdictional error for a human rights commission to set up an inquiry when the subject matter of the inquiry cannot involve a contravention of the Act ...

[34]    The Jewish complainant had alleged in a complaint to the Human Rights Commission that a particular school board fostered a climate in which anti-Jewish views were condoned and encouraged, thus depriving Jewish and other minority students of equality of opportunity with respect to education, a public service. The Commission investigated and recommended an inquiry; the Minister established a board of inquiry. The trial judge concluded that educational services did not come within "accommodation, services and facilities" as found in the legislation. The Court of Appeal decided otherwise. At the conclusion of his judgment, Chief Justice Stratton said at pp. 208–209 [D/6433, para. 45431]:

It is perhaps unnecessary to point out that it is the function of the board of inquiry and not of a reviewing court to investigate the merits of a complaint. I would, however, repeat the remarks of Thurlow, C.J., in the
Cummings
decision that in cases like the present one, it is usually preferable for the court to leave the tribunal free to carry out its mandate except when it is clear and beyond doubt that the tribunal is without jurisdiction to deal with the matter before it. In my opinion, the present case is not within the exception.

[35]    In the present case, it is uncontradicted that White was incapable of doing his job on February 22, 1991 (termination), on August 19, 1991 (filing of the complaint), and continually thereafter through March 25, 1993 (the establishment of the Board of Inquiry). Since April 1990, he has received total disability benefits from Workers' Compensation. He has not sought alternate employment because of his inability to do any work.

[36]    Section 9 of the
Code
states that "an employer ... shall not refuse to employ or to continue to employ or otherwise discriminate against a person in regard to employment ... because of that person's ... physical disability."

[37]    Two questions arise:

1.    Was White terminated "because of ... physical disability"?

2.    If so, was that termination discriminatory and thus in contravention of s. 9?

[38]    The latter question is clearly a question for the board of inquiry. The former question may be considered to involve, in the wording of
CIP Paper, supra,
at 616 "the decision as to whether the complaint is one which is contemplated by the pertinent legislation." However,
CIP Paper
involved a refusal to pay sick leave benefits on account of pregnancy-related illness. The complaint was discrimination in employment based on sex. In response to the allegation that the complaint was not based on sex, the Court of Appeal said that such a determination went to the merits of the case and should be decided by the board. It is not difficult to accept the view that whether or not employment actions based on pregnancy amount to discrimination based on sex is indeed a proper question for the specialized tribunal. The issue here is more straightforward, and, unlike most of the situations referred to in the authorities, the facts are uncontradicted. They are not the employer's facts, but they are the facts as provided by the complainant. White was incapable of doing his job. He was terminated one year after becoming incapable of doing his job; he remained incapable of doing that job for at least two more years.

[39]    Counsel for the Commission conceded that, if White were presenting as a person seeking employment, and given his inability to do the job, an employer who "refused to employ" White would not contravene the
Code.
She argued, however, that different considerations may apply to an existing employee, and that the refusal to continue to employ someone who was incapable because of disability may constitute discrimination. She suggested that a board could conclude that it was discriminatory to terminate White at that particular time, and that non-discriminatory conduct may necessitate the employer retaining White for a longer period than it actually did. Essentially, she argued that the board of inquiry is the appropriate forum to determine whether or not,
in
White
's particular circumstances, Woolco contravened the
Code
by terminating him as and when it did.

[40]    I do not agree that the concept and ambit of discrimination will vary depending on whether one is dealing with a person looking for work or a person actually employed. The fundamental purpose of the
Code
is to prevent discrimination against, in this case, the physically disabled. Surely, the protection of the
Code
is not to be limited only to certain categories of physically disabled persons. The principles of the
Code
require that a disabled person who is employed will not be discriminated against because of his or her physical disability; those principles also require that, if that same person were seeking to be employed, he or she is not to be discriminated against because of that physical disability.

[41]    In
Belliveau
v.
Steel Company of Canada
(1988),
1988 CanLII 8876 (ON HRT)
,
9 C.H.R.R. D/5250 (Ont.)
, the Board of Inquiry said, at [D/5251–D/5252] paras. 39569–70:

The
Code
seeks to secure equality of opportunity for the handicapped with respect to employment. Everyone is entitled to the same opportunity to make the most of his or her life, regardless of physical or mental handicap. Thus, an employer must make a decision respecting employment of a handicapped person based upon a fair and accurate assessment of his true ability, and not based upon a stereotype or misconception about a disability.

The law insists that every person receives a fair chance to show what he is able to do, taking into account his ability. The law protects every person from being pre-judged because of handicap by an employer. Equal opportunity for someone with a handicap means equal opportunity to do the things he can do effectively. The law does not impose any undue hardship upon the employer, or require that a person who presents a danger to the safety of the employee himself or others, be employed.

[42]    I note the wording in s. 9 — "... shall not refuse to employ or to continue to employ or
otherwise discriminate
" [emphasis added]. The prohibited conduct is discrimination — the refusal to employ or to continue to employ are simply examples of conduct in the employment context that may support a claim for discrimination if motivated by the prohibited grounds. A discussion of the reason for White's termination may suggest some circularity in cause and effect, but in my view it is clear that he was terminated because he was absolutely incapable of doing his job. It is of course true that he was absolutely incapable of doing his job because of a disability, but the fact remains that he was incapable of doing his job. Reverting to the situation of a disabled person seeking employment — if that person is incapable of doing the job sought, the person is rejected not because of the disability, but because he or she cannot do the job. To conclude otherwise would be an affront to common sense.

[43]
In
Bonner
v.
Ontario (Ministry of Health)

(1992),
1992 CanLII 14236 (ON HRT)
,
16 C.H.R.R. D/485 (Ont.)
, the Board of Inquiry dealt with a complaint from an employee who had been released at the end of his probationary period. It was conceded that the employee had a mental handicap; that handicap precluded the employee from adequately performing the requirements of his position. The Ontario
Code
[S.O. 1981, c. 53] contained a specific provision that a right under the
Code
was not infringed if a person, because of handicap, could not fulfil the essential requirements of the position. However, the Board expressed in general terms its view that an employee's inability to do the job, whether that inability flowed from a handicap or otherwise, posed no obligation on the employer to hire, retain or accommodate the employee in question.

At [D/49] paras. 82–83:

In my opinion, a person who by reason of handicap cannot work competently on a regular basis is incapable of satisfying the requirements of the position regardless of how he or she might perform when unaffected by that handicap. And, as was said in
Chamberlin
v.
599273 Ontario Ltd.

(1989),
1989 CanLII 9081 (ON HRT)
,
11 C.H.R.R. D/110
at D/116 [para. 36]:

[T]he Code does not ignore the fact that certain handicaps can negatively impact on an individual's ability to perform certain types of work. If a person is unable to adequately perform a particular job because of a handicap, the Code does not entitle that person to employment in the job. What the Code does do is ensure that persons with a handicap are not discriminated against with respect to jobs they are capable of performing.

The Commission's position appears as well to be based on the premise that what is to be accommodated is not the
handicap
per se
,
but the substandard performance caused thereby. The suggestion seems to be that, while a person who is unable to perform work for a reason other than handicap may be refused employment or fired, a person who is unable to perform that work because of a handicap as defined by the Code can be neither denied employment nor fired if that
inability
can be accommodated in the sense (apparently) of being tolerated. That premise seems plainly wrong. Surely that which must be accommodated if reasonably possible is the handicap, not the inability. It is the employee who must be reasonably assisted to satisfy the requirements of the work, rather than the work that must be modified to satisfy the requirements of the employee. If the employer can without undue hardship adjust the conditions of the workplace satisfactorily while subject to the effects of that handicap, then that must be done. But there is no requirement imposed on employers either to hire or to retain employees who, because of handicap, are in fact incapable of doing the work, simply because they have the resources to tolerate actually deficient work. [Emphasis in original.]

[44]    If White was incapable of doing his job, and was terminated for that reason, does that fact take his complaint outside the ambit of s. 9 of the
Code?
In my view, it does. Section 9 deals only with employment actions taken "because of" one or more prohibited grounds. If there is a dispute over whether a particular action was "because of" a particular ground, the Commission and perhaps a board of inquiry will deal with the matter.
In
White
's case, in February 1991, had he been capable of doing his job with, for example, some mechanical or other assistance, but had still been terminated, a legitimate question would arise whether or not White had been terminated "because of" physical disability.

[45]    But if, on the complainant's asserted facts, he was at the time of termination, at the time of the complaint, and at the time of establishment of a board, absolutely incapable of doing the job from which he had been terminated, there can be no real dispute. White was not terminated "because of" a physical disability. The employer's action was not based on a prohibited ground. Therefore, there is no possibility of a contravention of the
Code
and hence nothing on which to found the establishment of a board of inquiry.

[46]    Counsel for the Commission argued that a board of inquiry would, and should, properly consider whether or not Woolco was under an obligation to accommodate White, and whether or not, in failing to accommodate him, Woolco contravened s. 9. The short answer is, just as there is no duty to accommodate a person who is seeking employment and who is absolutely incapable of doing the job applied for, neither is there any duty to accommodate a present employee who is incapable of doing the job.

[47]    Unlike the legislation in some jurisdictions, the Newfoundland
Code
contains no statutory duty of accommodation. The employer's duty to accommodate in the absence of a specific statutory duty was considered in depth by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Central Alberta Dairy Pool
v.
Alberta (Human Rights Commission)
,

1990 CanLII 76 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R. 489
[12 C.H.R.R. D/417]. The complainant had been fired for being absent on a busy working day at a milk processing plant. He had earlier requested the day off to observe what was for him a holy day. The legislation in question was similar in content, although not in structure, to the Newfoundland
Code.
The Alberta legislation [
Individual's Rights Protection Act,
R.S.A. 1980, c. I-2] read:

7(1) No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall

(a)    refuse to employ or refuse to continue to employ any person, or

(b)    discriminate against any person with regard to employment or any term or condition of employment,

because of the race, religious beliefs, colour, sex, physical characteristics, marital status, age, ancestry or place of origin of that person or of any other person.

[48]    Wilson J., speaking for the majority of the Court, stated the issue as revolving around the designation of an employer rule as a
bona fide
occupational qualification under s. 7(3) of the Alberta
Act.
She characterized the rule, at p. 501 [D/424, para. 23]:

The complainant in the case at bar simply asked for one particular Monday off. Given this fact, the only way to characterize the respondent's rule would appear to be "mandatory attendance on Mondays except in case of illness or other emergencies, religious obligation not being included as an emergency for this purpose." Stated in the obverse, the rule prohibited Monday absences due to religious obligation.

[49]    Wilson J. reviewed previous Supreme Court of Canada decisions on the different concepts of discrimination and the relationship to those concepts of statutory justification (
bona fide
occupational qualification) and a duty to accommodate. My reading of her judgment suggests the following:

1.    In the employment context, discrimination may be either "direct" or "adverse effect."

2.    Direct discrimination occurs when an employer adopts a practice or a rule which on its face discriminates on a prohibited ground. An example would be a rule stating — "no disabled persons employed here."

3.    Direct discrimination is generally easily identified as a contravention of human rights legislation. However, the impugned rule may be justified if the employer can satisfy the tribunal that the rule is a
bona fide
occupational requirement, or, as in the Newfoundland
Code,
a good faith occupational qualification (subsection 9(1)). Such a qualification is related to the job and not to any individual employee. The duty to accommodate any particular individual employee does not arise in cases of direct discrimination or in the context of
bona fide
occupational qualifications. As Wilson J. said at p. 514 [D/433–D/434, para. 49]:

Where a rule discriminates on its face on a prohibited ground of discrimination, it follows that it must rely for its justification on the validity of its application to all members of the group affected by it. There can be no duty to accommodate individual members of that group within the justificatory test because, as McIntyre J. pointed out, that would undermine the rationale of the defence. Either it is valid to make a rule that generalizes about members of a group or it is not. By their very nature rules that discriminate directly impose a burden on all persons who fall within them. If they can be justified at all, they must be justified in their general application. That is why the rule must be struck down if the employer fails to establish the BFOQ.

4.    Adverse effect discrimination occurs when a rule which is neutral on its face has an adverse effect on one particular employee or group of employees because of a characteristic of that individual or group relating to a prohibited ground of discrimination. For example, the rule in question
in
Central Alberta Dairy Pool
, supra,
was a generally applicable neutral rule requiring attendance on Mondays. The singular adverse effect of the rule on the complainant resulted from his religious beliefs which precluded his working on the Monday in question. In this context, the neutral rule is upheld; it applies to everyone other than those on whom it has a discriminatory impact. It will only be applied to those individuals if the employer can demonstrate that it cannot accommodate those particular employees without undue hardship. Thus, where a neutral rule leads to adverse effect discrimination, a duty to accommodate arises. That duty will give way to proof of undue hardship by the employer.

The above discussion does not contemplate any statutory duty of accommodation.

[50]    There is clearly no issue of direct discrimination
in
White
's case. There is no evidence, nor any reference in the complaint to any rule at Woolco that on its face discriminated against the physically disabled.

[51]    Is there any basis for a complaint of adverse discrimination? If so, it would be for a board to consider whether such a complaint was made out, and to include in such consideration the extent of any duty to accommodate. The complaint does not allege the application to White of a rule "neutral on its face." It may be inferred that the general rule is that Woolco employees must be capable of coming to work and doing the job for which they are hired. This rule adversely affects all those who are incapable of doing their job, regardless of the reason, for that lack of ability. Any such rule, which is more properly considered not as a rule, but as the fundamental obligation of the employee in an employment relationship, is aimed at and is applied to the ability to do the job. It does not adversely affect any individual because of that individual's identification with a prohibited ground of discrimination.

[52]    There is therefore nothing
in
White
's complaint, when considered in light of the uncontradicted facts he provided, which could suggest an adverse effect "because of" physical disability. Hence, there is no possibility of any duty to accommodate.

[53]    Some may suggest that, given White's twenty-four years of service, Woolco perhaps has a duty to accommodate White by keeping him on as an employee beyond February 22, 1991, and that the Board of Inquiry must be given the opportunity to consider that issue.

[54]    The brief of the Commission includes the following:

7.    Additional issues that may be considered by the Board of Inquiry, depending on the evidence properly adduced in that forum, would include:

Did termination of employment
after less than one year
satisfy the good faith occupational qualification requirement?

If not, (i)
after what period of time
would the good faith occupational qualification be satisfied, and (ii) what remedy, including compensation for the discrimination, should be awarded?

Is the Plaintiff required to accommodate the Complainant?

If so, in what manner and to what extent? [Emphasis added.]

The references to "after less than one year" and "after what period of time," although written in the context of the good faith occupational qualification, in my view wrongly incorporate consideration of rights and remedies arising from the employment relationship and not from any contravention of the
Code.

[55]    A good faith occupational requirement is job related — it is in no sense related to nor its content shaped by the length of time that any particular individual has been on or off the job. A duty to accommodate arises when a neutral rule adversely affects any employee because of that employee's identification with a prohibited ground of discrimination. The duty is to accommodate the results that flow from the employee's identification with the prohibited ground, and, in my view, the extent of that duty must be uniform among all affected employees. The duty does not vary with the length of time that any particular employee has been employed; if an employee is incapable of working, and the employer acts accordingly, the issue of accommodation does not arise since there is no action because of a prohibited ground.

[56]    This latter conclusion may be readily tested. If a person absolutely incapable of doing a particular job due to a physical disability seeks to be employed to do that job, could it be suggested that the refusal of the employer contravenes the
Code,
in the sense of adverse effect discrimination, and that the employer therefore has a duty to accommodate the individual, up to a point of undue hardship? Even the most liberal interpretation of the
Code
cannot support this proposition. Actions taken because of a person's complete inability to do his or her job are not within the ambit of the
Code
and do not engage the adjudicative and remedial authority of a board of inquiry.

[57]    Actions taken by an employer because of a person's inability and failure to do a job — whether that inability or failure is caused by, for example, disability, incompetence, absenteeism or lack of necessary certification — are evaluated in the context of the particular employment relationship. Whether the employee is entitled to any remedy will depend on a court's assessment of all of the variables of that relationship, including the individual's particular circumstances such as age, length of service and the like. In this
case,
White
has pursued and received his civil remedy for his termination.

[58]    The
Code
does not deal with rights and obligations arising out of the contract of employment; it is concerned with the imposition on employers of a statutory standard of conduct. That standard is expected to be observed by employers in making decisions related to employment, whether before or after an individual is hired.

[59]    The fact that White's injury occurred at work does not heighten any obligation of the employer under the
Code.
The workers' compensation system is designed to provide redress for work-related injuries. The
Code
is aimed at conduct caused by one of the prohibited grounds. In the case of disability, the
Code
contemplates no examination of how the disability arose. It does not matter — the fact that a person is disabled is enough to engage the provisions of the
Code
and protect that person from being singled out because of that disability. My conclusion that the complaint does not fall within the prohibited grounds of s. 9 is not influenced by the fact that White was injured at work, nor by the fact that he has already been the beneficiary of an adjudication in Court. The facts are uncontradicted. White was not terminated because of a prohibited ground, and a board of inquiry has no jurisdiction to adjudicate his complaint.

Issue No. 2

[60]    Is the Commission required by the
Code
to attempt to effect a settlement of the complaint as a precondition to appointing a board of inquiry; if so, was such an attempt made in this case?

Positions of the Parties

[61]    Woolco argued that subsection 21(1) of the
Code
imposes on the Commission an obligation to attempt to settle a dispute. It further argued that such an attempt to settle is a precondition to any appointment of a board of inquiry. The Commission involved only one party in settlement discussions and hence did not fulfil its statutory obligation. It is therefore without jurisdiction to appoint a board of inquiry.

[62]    The Commission argued that settlement is not a statutory precondition to appointing a board of inquiry and that, in any event, an obligation to settle does not require that the Commission enter into discussions with both parties once one party has clearly indicated its intention not to settle.

Facts

[63]    Gladys Vivian, Executive Director of the Commission, deposed:

2.   In accordance with the ordinary procedure followed by the Human Rights Commission (the "Commission"), I forwarded all the documentation collected and generated during the Commission's investigation with respect to the complaint filed by Thomas White against Woolworth Canada Inc. to our solicitor, B. Gale Welsh, for her review, assessment and recommendation.

3.   Ms. Welsh responded with her assessment and recommendation in a memorandum addressed to me, dated February 1, 1993 (the "memorandum").

4.   In the memorandum, Ms. Welsh recommended that further discussions regarding settlement be undertaken with the Complainant.

5.   A proposal for settlement, together with an explanation, was set out in the memorandum.

7.   On February 8, 1993, at the offices of the Commission, I met with Patricia Corbett, Investigating Officer with the Commission, Thomas White, the Complainant, and Michael Crosbie, Solicitor for the Complainant.

8.   The purpose of the February 8, 1993 meeting (the "meeting") was to have the Complainant reconsider his position on settlement.

12.  The Commission's settlement proposal, discussed at the meeting, was rejected by the Complainant.

13.  In view of the Complainant's rejection of the proposal, I did not contact the Plaintiff regarding the memorandum.

Ms. Corbett's case record notes:

Gladys & I met with Tom White & his solicitor Michael Crosbie on 93-02-08. We discussed Gail's recommendation with them and participated in a lengthy discussion of same. They were not willing to accept her recommendations. It is my understanding that Michael or Tom will put something in writing to the Commissioners.

[64]    White's solicitor then provided a submission to the Commission, and on March 25, the Commission appointed a board of inquiry. The Commission's last contact with Woolco had been on December 1, 1992, when it received from Woolco a reply to an earlier request for information. Woolco had no knowledge of the settlement proposal of Ms. Welsh, nor of the discussions between the Commission, White and his solicitor. Woolco was not asked for its views on settlement, nor advised of White's position.

The Code

65    21(1)     Where a complaint is filed with the executive director, the executive director or a person designated by the executive director shall investigate the complaint and try to settle the matter.

(3) Following an investigation, the executive director shall make a report to the commission and the commission may determine whether or not to refer the matter to a board of inquiry.

23(1) Where the executive director, or a person designated by the executive director, effects a settlement of a complaint he or she shall report the settlement to the commission.

(2) Where the report referred to in subsection (1) is approved by the commission, the executive director shall notify the parties that no further action will be taken with regard to the complaint unless the terms of a settlement are not complied with.

(3) Where the terms of a settlement referred to in subsection (1) or (4) are not complied with, the commission may reopen the complaint and proceed as if a settlement had not been effected.

(4) A complaint shall be considered settled for the purpose of this Act only if the commission approves the settlement and agrees to its terms.

Analysis

66    Counsel for the Commission pointed out that the
Code
does not contain any explicit reference in subsection 21(3) to settlement not being effected before a board may be appointed. However, looking at both ss. 21 and 23, it is apparent that the only situation to which subsection 21(3) would apply is one where settlement has not been achieved. Under s. 23, the Commission must receive a report of any settlement. If the Commission approves the settlement, no further action is taken on the complaint, unless the terms of the settlement are not complied with. Once settlement has been reached, the statute contemplates the Commission's approving the settlement; there is no suggestion at all that the Commission would consider appointment of a board of inquiry once settlement has been reached. The only reasonable construction of subsection 21(3) is that "the Commission may determine whether or not to refer the matter to a board of inquiry" only when settlement has not been effected.

[67]    The obligation imposed on the executive director by subsection 21(1) "... shall investigate the complaint and try to settle the matter" omits the word "shall" before "try to settle." It is obvious that the omission is simply to avoid repetition. The intent is clear — the executive director shall investigate the complaint and [shall] try to settle the matter. The word "shall" is imperative (
Interpretation Act,
R.S.N. 1990, c. I-19, subsection 11(2)).

[68]    The executive director is required to try to reach a settlement. Is fulfilment of this obligation a precondition to any determination by the Commission to refer the complaint to a board of inquiry? In my opinion, it is.

[69]    The
Code
goes to some lengths to set out a procedure for the reporting of a settlement to the Commission, the Commission's approval of any settlement, and for the reopening of any complaint if settlement terms are broken. The
Code
contemplates a settlement as a meaningful alternative to formal adjudication of the complaint.

[70]    The attention given to settlement in the
Code
reflects one of the Commission's responsibilities under s. 18:

18.  The commission shall

(b)    promote an understanding of, acceptance of and compliance with this Act;

[71]    Settlement discussions are one means of promoting an understanding of and compliance with the principles of the
Code.
Indeed, settlement discussions are far more likely to promote this objective than the blunt weapon of adjudication by a board of inquiry.

[72]    The legislation establishes the board of inquiry as a last resort to be used only if settlement is not possible. If this were not so, why would the
Code
direct the executive director to try to settle the matter? The specific reference to settlement confirms that it is an essential part of the complaint process. Settlement must be attempted before the Commission can determine whether a board of inquiry is warranted.

[73]    The Alberta Court of Appeal considered the obligation to attempt settlement
in
Alberta Human Rights Commission
v.
Pro Western Plastics Ltd.
,

1983 ABCA 185 (CanLII)
,
[1983] 5 W.W.R. 730
[
1983 CanLII 4706 (AB CA)
,
4 C.H.R.R. D/1579
]. The employer complained against refused to meet with the Commission until it received information on the nature of the complaints and the surrounding facts. The Commission concluded that the employer had refused to consider settlement and appointed a board of inquiry. The employer sought to quash the decision appointing the board.

[74]    The Alberta legislation made specific reference to the failure to reach a settlement:

27(1) If the commission is unable to effect a settlement of the matter complained of, it shall report to the Minister and may, in its discretion, direct that a formal inquiry into the matter be held by a board of inquiry.

[75]    As I have indicated above, although there is no similar phrase in the Newfoundland
Code,
the authority to appoint a board nonetheless applies only where no settlement has been reached. In
Pro Western Plastics, supra,
the majority quashed the order. Stevenson J.A. did so on the ground that the appeal was moot, while Haddad J.A. concluded that the requirement to attempt settlement was a precondition to the appointment of a board. He wrote, at p. 738 [D/1580, para. 13601], that if the condition had not been satisfied:

... then the appointment is without jurisdiction and ineffective. De Smith in his work
Judicial Review of Administrative Action,
4th ed. (1980), at p. 115 says:

... it is clearly proper for a superior court to hold that an inferior tribunal lacks jurisdiction to embark on an inquiry unless the stage has been properly set ...

It cannot be said that the stage has been properly set in this matter unless the appellant has fulfilled the statutory conditions for the appointment of the board.

[76]    On his review of the facts, Haddad J.A. concluded that the employer had not refused to consider settlement, but that it had made reasonable inquiries of the Commission and (at p. 746 [D/1583, para. 13618]) "... was entitled to a proper response to allow it to assess its position before entering into settlement negotiations."

[77]    Haddad J.A. concluded at p. 746 [D/1583, paras. 13620–21]:

"Inability" [to effect a settlement] only occurs when a person against whom a complaint is made is unwilling to negotiate in good faith, or at all, or after two parties negotiating in good faith are unable to reach terms mutually acceptable.

In my view the learned trial judge rightly concluded that the evidence did not establish that the commission has arrived at the point where the inability to effect a settlement existed. The stage for the appointment of a board of inquiry had not been properly set, and for that reason the appointment became a nullity.

[78]    Was settlement attempted in this case?

The Commission's Executive Director and investigator met with White and his solicitor and discussed "in some detail" the settlement options proposed by the Commission's solicitor. Settlement on the basis proposed was rejected out of hand by White, and the process stopped there.

[79]    Presenting a suggestion to one party and then giving up when that party rejects the suggestion does not satisfy the obligation imposed by the
Code.
A meaningful settlement process must involve communication with more than one side to the dispute. While the process need not involve both parties meeting face to face, the settlement effort required by the
Code
surely contemplates some discussion between the Commission and each party. The process of settlement is one of negotiation and give and take — the
Code
requires a
bona fide
effort on the part of the executive director to facilitate that process. The obligation on the executive director is not satisfied by the simple rejection of a proposal presented to one party by the Commission, while throughout the other party is kept completely in the dark. Without defining the parameters of the obligation to try to bring about a settlement, it includes at least, in these circumstances, the duty to actively consider other options if a first proposal is rejected out of hand. It also includes the duty to involve both parties to the dispute.

[80]    The statutory obligation to try to bring about a settlement was not satisfied in this case. Until that obligation was met, the Commission lacked the jurisdiction to consider the appointment of a board of inquiry.

Issue No. 3

[81]    Did the Commission act fairly and without creating a reasonable apprehension of bias in its dealings with the complainant prior to constituting a board of inquiry?

Positions of the Parties

[82]    Woolco argued that the Commission breached the rules of procedural fairness in not giving to Woolco opportunities given to White to influence the decision-making process. Woolco suggested the following shortcomings:

(i)    The failure to provide Woolco with a copy of the Investigator's report of July 2, 1992;

(ii)   The failure to give Woolco the opportunity to participate in settlement discussions and to review the recommendations and report of the Commission's solicitor;

(iii)  The failure to give Woolco the opportunity to make submissions to the Commission prior to the Commission's deciding to appoint a board of inquiry.

[83]    Woolco argued that these breaches of fair procedure are sufficient to void the decision to appoint a board of inquiry. Woolco further suggested that these breaches also raise a reasonable apprehension of bias in the exercise of the Commission's power to appoint a board, thus tainting that decision to the point where it cannot be allowed to stand.

[84]    The Commission took the position that, had Woolco taken initiatives similar to those of White's solicitor, it could readily have involved itself in the process. Since the filing of the complaint, Woolco's record of responding to requests for information had been abysmal, and the processing of the complaint should not be prejudiced by giving Woolco more opportunity to delay the process. The Commission suggested that, in any event, procedural fairness does not require that the Commission give parties the opportunity to make submissions to the Commission before the decision to appoint a board of inquiry.

Facts

[85]    Woolco received notice of the complaint in August 1991. Within Woolco the complaint "fell between the cracks." A number of people, including in-house solicitors, were involved from time to time. The Commission periodically requested information for its investigation; Woolco took months to respond. In the latter stages of the investigation, Ms. Gortler, a solicitor with Woolco, assumed responsibility for Woolco's response to the complaint. On October 16, 1992, Ms. Corbett wrote to Woolco requesting certain information. Ms. Gortler provided that information on December 1, 1992. That was the last communication to or from Woolco until after the board of inquiry was appointed.

[86]    As noted earlier, on February 8, 1993, Vivian and Corbett met with White and his solicitor. The Commission arranged the meeting in order to pursue with White the possibility of a settlement. At the meeting, White and his solicitor were given the opportunity to read the memorandum prepared by the Commission's solicitor. As Gladys Vivian said in her affidavit:

9.   At the meeting, for the purpose of advancing our discussions on settlement, I permitted Michael Crosbie [White's solicitor] to read the memorandum.

White was also given a copy of the Commission investigator's report of July 2, 1992. This was later mailed to him because he left it at the meeting.

[87]    Vivian deposed:

16.  It was the policy of the Commission not to distribute copies of the Investigator's Report unless requested by a party.

The letter forwarding the report to White said:

Dear Mr. White:

Enclosed please find a copy of the formal report on this complaint. Also enclosed is additional information from Elaine Gortler, solicitor for Woolco, which arrived after the report was written.

If you wish to respond to the enclosed documentation, please have your written response submitted by March 20, 1993.

Yours truly,

Patricia Corbett, B.A.
Human Rights Investigator.

[88]    On March 16, 1993, by letter addressed to the members of the Commission, White's solicitor forwarded a lengthy submission outlining why, in his view, the complaint was made out and why a board of inquiry should be established. Counsel for White candidly admitted that the purpose of sending the submission was to "persuade the Commission of the rightness of my client's case."

[89]    On March 25, the Commission appointed the board of inquiry.

Analysis

[90]    The facts are uncontradicted. The Commission gave White opportunities to review Commission documentation and make submissions to the Commission. The Commission gave Woolco no such opportunity. Whether or not Woolco would have availed [itself] of any opportunity is irrelevant; similarly, whether Woolco could and should have acted on its own initiative is not relevant. The issue is simply whether the Commission, by giving one party opportunities not given to the other, has so tainted its decision-making process that the decision reached cannot stand.

[91]    A decision of a human rights commission to appoint a board of inquiry is not a decision to be taken lightly. The Commission's authority during the investigative stage is extensive. Of itself, a decision following investigation to constitute an inquiry suggests that the complaint may be well founded. Preparation for and attendance at an inquiry requires each party to invest time and other resources. Since the Commission has carriage of the complaint (para. 26(1)(a)), the more severe burden is on the respondent. The scope of an inquiry may extend well beyond the facts surrounding the complaint to include a wider analysis of the respondent's policies and practices. The Board is vested with all the coercive powers bestowed by the
Public Inquiries Act
[R.S.N. 1990, c. P-38]. Most significantly, the constitution of a board of inquiry makes available a virtually unlimited range of remedies:

[92]    Subsection 28(1)(b) of the
Code:

28(1) A board of inquiry

(b)    may, where it finds that a complaint is justified in whole or in part, order the person against whom the finding was made to do 1 or more of the following:

(i)    to stop the contravention complained of,

(ii)    to refrain in future from committing the same or a similar contravention,

(iii)    to make available to the person discriminated against the rights, opportunities or privileges he or she was denied contrary to this Act,

(iv)    to provide compensation to the person discriminated against, including compensation for all or a part of wages or income lost or expenses incurred because of the discriminatory action, and

(v)    to take whatever other action the board considers appropriate.

[93]    The establishment of a board of inquiry is a decision that must be taken with full understanding of its potential consequences. A respondent is called before an inquiry to face unknown consequences. Any decision to invoke the adjudication of a board must be taken, and be seen to be taken, in a fair and even-handed manner. The Commission invited White and his solicitor to meet and discuss Ms. Welsh's recommendations; it provided White with the investigator's report; it invited White to make a submission to the Commission before a decision was taken to appoint a board. Not a word was said to Woolco, the party most at risk in an adjudication. Woolco was not offered the opportunity to persuade the Commission that a board should not be convened.

[94]    I express no opinion on whether the duty of fairness requires the Commission to invite the parties to make submissions before a board is appointed. The difficulty in this case is the preferential treatment given to one party. To a reasonable observer, offering only to one party the opportunity to influence the decision to appoint a board would offend basic principles of fairness. It is impossible to conclude that the decision to appoint a board was taken in circumstances that inspired an assurance of impartiality and awareness of respect for the rights of those at risk. The appearance is the reverse. The breach of the duty of fair procedure is not excused by Woolco's delay in responding to requests from the Commission. As of December 1, 1992, there were no requests to which Woolco had not responded. Even if there had been, that does not give the Commission the right to give to only one party the opportunity to influence the process. Whether or not Woolco would have responded is not the point; the preference of opportunity given to White, together with his access to Commission documents, taints the subsequent decision to appoint a board of inquiry.

[95]    The procedure followed by the Commission also raises a reasonable apprehension of bias in the Commission's decision to appoint a board of inquiry. This is of course closely linked to the issue of procedural fairness. The Commission operated closely with White and his solicitor in the course of the investigation. White had access not only to the investigator's report, but also to the memorandum prepared for the Commission by its solicitor. The Commission invited, and received, a lengthy memorandum urging White's position on the Commission. The latter stages of the Commission's investigation, up to and including the decision to appoint the Board, can be readily perceived as a joint effort on the part of the Commission and White, to the complete exclusion of Woolco. A reasonable observer could conclude that the decision to appoint a board was a foregone conclusion, and was simply a formality to be effected so that White and the Commission could further pursue the complaint against Woolco.

[96]    The breaches of procedural fairness and the raising of a reasonable apprehension of bias are sufficient in my view to preclude the Commission from proceeding further with the complaint.

FAILURE TO PRODUCE THE SOLICITOR'S REPORT

[97]    The Commission's solicitor produced a memorandum on February 1, 1993. It was addressed and forwarded to Vivian. Vivian deposed:

4.    In the memorandum, Ms. Welsh recommended that further discussions regarding settlement be undertaken with the Complainant.

5.    A proposal for settlement, together with an explanation, was set out in the memorandum.

6.    The only additional point covered in the memorandum is a list of three questions requiring consideration by the Commission should a settlement not be negotiated.

9.    At the meeting, for the purpose of advancing our discussions in settlement, I permitted Michael Crosbie [White's solicitor] to read the memorandum.

Neither Crosbie nor White received a copy of the memorandum.

[98]    Once litigation commenced, the solicitor for Woolco discovered the existence of the memorandum. He requested its production and was refused. The memorandum was not provided by the Commission in the return of its record to the Court under r. 54.08(1) of the Rules of the Supreme Court, 1986.

[99]    The Commission argued that the memorandum was a confidential communication made in the context of settlement discussions. Accordingly, and in order to facilitate the settlement process, the public interest requires that documents produced and discussions held in the settlement process be without prejudice and not subject to later production. The Commission also argued that production was precluded by subsection 31(1) of the
Code:

31(1) A member of the commission or a person employed in the administration of this Act shall not be required to give evidence or produce records obtained in the course of an investigation under this Act in a proceeding, except

(a)    to a board of inquiry appointed under this Act to deal with a matter to which that information is relevant; or

(b)    in an appeal under section 30 of this Act.

[100]    On the other hand, Woolco suggested that the document was prepared by the Commission's solicitor as a basis for a settlement between both sides, and that if one side had access to the document, surely any possible privilege residing with the Commission had been waived. Further, Woolco pointed out that, as stated in para. 6 of Vivian's affidavit, the document went beyond settlement issues to set out three matters requiring consideration by the Commission in its decision to appoint a board; White and his solicitor were aware of these issues, but Woolco was not. In any event, Woolco argued that the memorandum should at least have been produced to the Court under r. 54.08.

[101]    It is not necessary to rule on this issue. My earlier determinations have disposed of the application. A decision on the relationship of subsection 31(1) of the
Code
and r. 54.08 of the Rules of Court remains for a proper case.

SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS

102    1.    White was terminated because of his admitted absolute inability to do his job. The action of the employer was not "because of" a prohibited ground under the
Code;
there is no possible contravention of the
Code
on which to ground the appointment of a board of inquiry.

2.    An attempt by the Commission to effect settlement between the parties is a statutory precondition to the appointment of a board of inquiry. The Commission's actions did not amount to a
bona fide
attempt to settle, and the precondition for appointment of a board was not met.

3.    The actions of the Commission in dealing with White and his solicitor, to the exclusion of Woolco, including providing the investigator's report, allowing access to the solicitor's memorandum, and inviting a written submission to the Commission on the appointment of a board, breach the requirements of procedural fairness and raise a reasonable apprehension of bias in the decision to appoint a board of inquiry.

The decision of the Commission appointing a board of inquiry is quashed and the Commission is prohibited from proceeding further with the complaint.

COSTS

103    White supported the position of the Commission. This is understandable and to be expected. However, the litigation was not of White's making. While the seed of the litigation was of course White's complaint, he should not be penalized for exercising his statutory right to file a complaint. Neither should he be penalized because his solicitor quite properly took initiatives and took advantage of every opportunity offered.

[104]    This litigation was precipitated solely by the Commission's handling of the complaint. By refusing to recognize, and to so advise White, that his complaint was ill-founded, by joining forces with White against Woolco in the investigative and "settlement" stages, and by forging ahead to appoint a board of inquiry having invited only White to influence the decision, the Commission ran roughshod over the rights of Woolco and virtually invited this application. The
Code
properly imposes obligations on employers and others, but the principles of the
Code
and the interests it protects are in no way advanced when the body charged with safeguarding those principles acts as the Commission did here.

[105]    Both Woolco and White shall have their costs as against the Commission on a solicitor and his own client basis, my intention being that both Woolco and White will be fully reimbursed for their solicitor's fees and related disbursements reasonably incurred in connection with this application.

Order accordingly.
